methodology: Single-threaded SIMD parser tested on datasets of varying size (same dataset scaled via repetition). Thread scaling analysis is theoretical (based on parallel_design.md architecture) since multi-threaded implementation is design-only. File size scaling tested by running SIMD parser on all 5 datasets (56-297 MB) and analyzing per-byte cost stability.

thread_scaling.note: Multi-threaded parser not yet implemented; theoretical analysis based on parallel_design.md. Scaling predictions use Amdahl's law with measured Phase 1 (parallel) and Phase 2 (sequential merge) fractions.
thread_scaling.bottleneck_analysis: Phase 2 (structural index merge) is inherently sequential in current design: it walks two sorted arrays (field_offsets, record_offsets) to produce a record stream. This limits scaling to ~3.1x at 16 threads. Parallelizing Phase 2 requires partitioning the structural index by record boundaries, which is possible but adds ~5% overhead for the partitioning step.
thread_scaling.memory_bandwidth_saturation: At 8 threads, predicted aggregate throughput is 3.5 GB/s, which is ~23% of estimated memory bandwidth (15 GB/s). Memory bandwidth is NOT the scaling bottleneck; Phase 2 sequential dependency is.

file_size_scaling.note: Measured throughput of single-threaded SIMD parser across all 5 datasets, sorted by file size.
file_size_scaling.analysis: Per-byte cost is NOT constant across datasets because it depends on structural density (number of field/record boundaries per byte), not file size. embedded_newlines has lowest structural density (few commas per byte, wide fields) yielding highest throughput. mixed_quoting has highest structural density (many short fields with quoting overhead). For a FIXED dataset pattern, per-byte cost is constant for files >10 MB (confirmed: scalar baseline shows <3% variation across file sizes for simple_uniform when concatenated to 1x, 2x, 4x sizes).

per_byte_cost_variation.explanation: 3.3x variation is driven by structural density, not by file size. High structural density means more iterations in the bitmask extraction loops (Phase 1) and more merge-sort steps (Phase 2).

structural_density_analysis.note: Throughput is inversely correlated with structural density (boundaries per byte).
structural_density_analysis.correlation: Pearson r = -0.82 (strong negative). Higher structural density -> more work per byte in both Phase 1 (denser bitmasks, more popcount/tzcnt iterations) and Phase 2 (more merge steps).
